articleTitle: A review of precision AC voltage and current measurements
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Precision AC Voltage and Current Measurements Up to 1 MHz (Digest No: 1997/161)
abstract: Technological changes affecting the AC voltage measurements are discussed. These have been in both commercial instruments and in the potential for new standards. The main changes are: (a) the improved stability and increased range of commercial instruments; (b) the requirements for the calibration of non sinusoidal waveforms; (c) the potential for improved national standards for AC voltage generation and measurement. These changes lead to requirements for the extension in range of present calibration facilities for AC voltage as well as AC/DC transfer. There is also a requirement for the calibration of non sinusoidal waveforms. The development of new standards will initially support existing standards and ultimately provide better standards and better traceability to the primary DC standards. The Josephson array system could provide a primary standard of AC voltage. At NPL the AC voltage standard will provide a working standard which will provide the starting point for the extension to other voltages and frequencies.

publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Precision AC Voltage and Current Measurements Up to 1 MHz (Digest No: 1997/161)
abstract: This paper presents a series of randomly chosen examples from the author's 25 years of involvement in circuit design for precision AC measurement. A general view of the extraordinary difficulties in attempting to achieve levels of measurement accuracy in AC comparable with those commonly achieved in DC is presented. The examples discussed all gave problems but in most cases finally were cured, often with valuable insight gained.

publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Precision AC Voltage and Current Measurements Up to 1 MHz (Digest No: 1997/161)
abstract: All measurements are tainted by imperfectly known errors, so the significance associated with the result of a measurement must account for this uncertainty. This paper explores the reasoning behind, and the requirements for, the expression of a value of uncertainty associated with AC voltage measurements.

articleTitle: An AC voltage standard using digital synthesis
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Precision AC Voltage and Current Measurements Up to 1 MHz (Digest No: 1997/161)
abstract: With state of the art electronic components it seems possible that a digitally synthesised AC voltage standard can be constructed with uncertainties comparable with the best multi-junction thermal converters. Future work at NPL aims to improve uncertainties to a target of 0.1. p.p.m. over an increased voltage and frequency range. The prospect of traceable non-sinusoidal waveforms is also being investigated. It is envisaged that this technology will be used to improve traceability for harmonic and 'power' analysers as well as arbitrary waveform generators.

publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Precision AC Voltage and Current Measurements Up to 1 MHz (Digest No: 1997/161)
abstract: UKAS AC Voltage calibration accreditations have evolved progressively in the last 30 years. For the majority of this time UKAS electrical calibration accreditations have relied on one or two well known AC-DC Thermal Transfer Standards. However in recent years Electronic Reference Standards have been developed and the previous monopoly of thermal transfer standards is now challenged. Improved uncertainties of measurement are being sought from the National Physical Laboratory (NPL) by UKAS accredited laboratories so that they can improve their capabilities.

articleTitle: The significance of distortion and crest factors in AC measurements
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Precision AC Voltage and Current Measurements Up to 1 MHz (Digest No: 1997/161)
abstract: The uncertainty of any AC measurement is increased when the signal departs from a perfect sine wave. Depending on the nature of the distortion, it may be convenient to examine the problem in the frequency or time domain. When a waveform is distorted from the ideal sine form, harmonics are present. These can be identified and quantified by carrying out a Fourier analysis of the waveform. The consequences of harmonic content can be evaluated using the above expressions. A selection of results for typical levels of individual harmonics is given. It is emphasised that rms value is much less influenced by harmonic content than other measurements. The effects of active circuits are discussed pointing out that exact details of the source are important.
